title: Sprained Ankle
claims: An ankle sprain occurs when the ligaments supporting the ankle stretch beyond their limits and tear; severity depends on the number of ligaments involved and how much they are torn.

Symptoms include pain at rest and with weightbearing or activity, swelling, bruising, tenderness to touch, and instability or a feeling that the ankle gives out; severe sprain symptoms resemble a broken bone and require prompt medical evaluation.
An ankle sprain is largely a clinical diagnosis based on injury history, symptoms, and examination; X-rays or MRI are ordered to rule out a fracture or injury to nearby tendons and cartilage.

Grade 1 is slight stretching and microscopic tearing with mild tenderness, bruising and swelling, typically no pain with weightbearing, and no instability; Grade 2 is a partial tear with moderate swelling and bruising, mild weightbearing pain, and slight instability; Grade 3 is a complete tear with significant weightbearing pain and much instability.

Most isolated low ankle sprains heal without surgery through a three-phase program: short immobilization/rest/ice with early weightbearing as tolerated; range-of-motion, isometric strengthening and proprioception; then advanced strengthening and balance work with gradual return, starting with non-cutting activities before cutting sports.

Home RICE advice: rest the ankle; ice 20 to 30 minutes, 3 or 4 times daily, with a towel or pack barrier; compression dressing or wrap; elevate above heart level as often as possible during the first 48 hours.
A Grade 3 sprain may require a short leg cast or cast-brace for 10 to 14 days; the three-phase program may take about 2 weeks for minor sprains or 6 to 12 weeks for more severe injuries.

MRI is not required to diagnose ankle sprains; it may be ordered to assess ligaments, cartilage or tendons, for signs of a high ankle sprain, or if symptoms continue beyond 6 to 8 weeks despite conservative treatment.
Incomplete rehabilitation is the most common cause of chronic ankle instability; stopping strengthening exercises weakens the injured ligaments and raises the risk of repeat sprains.
A runner should be seen by a professional if the ankle remains swollen or painful for several weeks despite conservative treatment, or if there is trouble putting weight on the ankle.
Prevention rests on maintaining muscle strength, balance and flexibility: thorough warm-up, strengthening exercises for ankle stability, and supportive footwear.
